notes: This book has no relation to the deuterocanonical 1/2 Maccabees despite the near-identical name - the Ethiopian "Book of Meqabyan" (Meqabyan I, II, III) is a wholly separate composition, and this installment's title character "Meqabees" is not a Jewish freedom-fighter but a Moabite king who is God's chosen instrument to conquer and chastise a sinning Israel (ch.1), before himself entering genuine repentance at the prophet Re'ay's rebuke (ch.2-3) and becoming a model of righteous Gentile kingship (ch.4). Structurally the book is front-loaded with just eight chapters of real narrative (Meqabees' conquest/repentance, then his five children's martyrdom under the Chaldean king Tseerutsaydan) followed by thirteen chapters (9-21) of sustained theological discourse on bodily resurrection and the Day of Judgement, prompted by the martyred children's post-death appearance in ch.6-7 - these later chapters are addressed in direct second person ("unu"/"thou") to skeptics and to kings/nobles in general, but the text never re-tags a specific human speaker the way it named the prophet Re'ay in ch.2, so every law/theme tier in chapters 9-21 below is marked deliveredBy: null rather than guessing at an attribution the text doesn't give. The five children who are martyred are never given individual names, so they are indexed here as a single collective manager rather than as invented individuals, matching the book's own treatment of them as one unit throughout. Chapter 14 preserves a genuinely distinctive piece of content: three separate, explicitly attributed positions on the afterlife (Sadducee/Seduqan denial of any resurrection, Samaritan/Samran denial that flesh specifically can rise, and Pharisee/Fereesan belief in a different Heavenly flesh rather than the buried body) that the book answers point by point - a level of detail not present in the standard KJV canon. One reference (3:19, "the Nine Laws") appears to name a specific Moabite legal code contrasted with Torah law, but the text never defines its contents further, so it is left unglossed rather than guessed at. Naming note: "Mussie" (Moses) and "Aron" (Aaron) appear only as cited historical exempla within the resurrection discourse, not as characters personally embodied within this book's own narrative, so - matching the Leviticus/Deuteronomy precedent - they are logged in genealogyLists as bulk references rather than given full character entries here.

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Two Roads of the Soul

characters.name: Meqabees

children: Five unnamed sons - see the Five Martyred Children of Meqabees entry

verses.note: The Moabite king Meqabees, allied with Syria, Edom, and Amalek, conquers Israel from Iyabboq to Jerusalem as God's chosen instrument of chastisement against a sinning nation.
Musters from his home region of Riemat (Moab), besieges the Mesopotamia-to-Syria region, and defiles Jerusalem.
His army commits atrocities against captives, including children, widows, and the unborn, then returns home celebrating with feasting and song.
The prophet Re'ay warns him that JAH will punish him with sickness, not by the sword he trusts in.
Meqabees begins to mourn, wearing dust and sackcloth before JAH because of his sin.
Digs a pit, stands in it up to his neck, and weeps in genuine repentance.
JAH forgives him through the prophet's word; he swears to abandon idol worship for the sake of the children he fathered.
Destroys the idols and sorcery in his own household, and has the Israelite children he captured teach him and his people JAH's Law and Commandments.

Fully adopts Israel's sacrifices, tithes, and feasts; is never again defeated in battle once he trusts JAH instead of idols; dies in old age after a life of generosity to the poor, widows, and orphans.

funFacts: Despite the near-identical name, this Meqabees is a Moabite king, not to be confused with the Maccabees of the deuterocanonical books - the Ethiopian 'Book of Meqabyan' (I-III) is an entirely separate composition with an unrelated story.
He is described as originally undefeatable in his own eyes through idol-worship, but only becomes genuinely unconquerable in battle after his conversion to worshipping JAH.

characters.name: Re'ay (the Prophet)

verses.note: Delivers JAH's oracle of coming chastisement to Meqabees, warning that sickness - not warfare - will be his punishment.
Travels from Yihuda's Riemat region to find Meqabees weeping in his self-dug pit.
Relays JAH's acceptance of Meqabees' repentance, and personally instructs him to abandon idolatry and know JAH.

funFacts: His name 'Re'ay' functions in the text as a title/name (the text calls him simply 'the prophet whom them call Re'ay') - no longer proper name, tribe, or genealogy is ever given for him.

characters.name: The Five Children of Meqabees

verses.note: After Meqabees dies, his young children rule righteously for five years, caring for orphans and widows as their father taught them.
The Chaldean king Tseerutsaydan invades, destroys their country, and takes them captive.
Unlike their captors, they refuse to eat carrion, blood, or anything sacrificed to idols.
Refuse Tseerutsaydan's demand to sacrifice to the idol Bi'iel Fiegor; are bound, insulted, and burned alive in a fire for their faith.
After their death, they appear to Tseerutsaydan at night bearing drawn swords, terrifying him.
Deliver a post-mortem speech to the king, condemning him, his idols, and his priests to Gehenna.
Their willingness to die rather than eat the forbidden sacrifice is held up as the model of true faith in bodily resurrection, since they believed a later, greater life awaited them.

funFacts: The text never gives the five children individual names - they are consistently narrated and quoted as a single unit, so they are indexed here as one collective figure rather than as five invented identities.
Their post-death appearance and speech (ch. 6-7) is the direct narrative occasion for the book's long teaching on bodily resurrection that fills chapters 9-21.

characters.name: Tseerutsaydan

verses.note: The Chaldean king conquers Meqabees' land, plunders it, and takes his children captive to a foreign country.
Installs false priests and idols, sacrificing to Bi'iel Fiegor morning and evening.
Orders the five captive children burned alive when they refuse to sacrifice to his idols.
Is seized with terror when the dead children appear before him at night, and begs them not to take his life.

Continues an ever-escalating career of conquest and pride, described in language echoing the arrogant kings taunted in Isaiah and Daniel's iron-kingdom vision, boasting that his own era 'became like unto the Sun era.'
Is directly addressed and warned that his authority itself was given by JAH and can just as easily be taken away.
Dies suddenly, struck down mid-boast by the Angel of Death; his own kingdom is then destroyed and plundered in turn.

funFacts: Chapters 8-9 describe his career and downfall in language closely paralleling the Isaiah 14 taunt against the king of Babylon and Daniel's iron-kingdom imagery, though the text never explicitly identifies him with either of those figures.

The text calls Satan (Deeyablos) his rhetorical 'father' and 'teacher' (e.g. 6:22, 9:2, 9:4) purely as a condemnation of his character - this is a figure of speech in the text, not a literal genealogical claim, and is not recorded as such in his genealogy field here.

characters.name: Thilimyakos, the Angel of Death

verses.note: The named Angel of Death strikes Tseerutsaydan dead in an instant, mid-boast about his own supposed immortality.

funFacts: Appears in only a single verse, but unlike most agents of judgement elsewhere in the book, is given a real proper name.

characters.name: The Idol Priests of Bi'iel Fiegor

verses.note: Priests Tseerutsaydan appoints to serve the idol Bi'iel Fiegor; pressure the captive children of Meqabees to sacrifice and eat the forbidden offering, and report their refusal to the king.

funFacts: Never individually named - the text treats them as a serving office/collective, so they are indexed here as one entry rather than as invented individuals.

characters.name: Balaam's Curse (teaching)
characters.purpose: A direct warning to 'the nobles and the kings' not to walk Satan's road of pride, built from two Torah precedents: Balak son of Zippor hiring the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, who could only bless what God had already blessed; and Moses' humble intercession for the brother and sister who criticized him, set against Korah's company being swallowed by the earth for rebelling against him - concluding with a summary of the Tabernacle worship Moses and Aaron established and its continuation through Eli, Samuel, and Solomon.

verses.note: Warns Tseerutsaydan that his authority was given by God and can be revoked.
Recounts Balak hiring Balaam to curse Israel, and Balaam's refusal to curse a people God has blessed.
Balaam refuses Balak's offer of silver and gold rather than curse Israel.
Praises Moses' humility in interceding for his own accusers, contrasted with Korah's company being swallowed by the earth.
Summarizes Moses and Aaron building the Tabernacle's furnishings, and the priesthood's continued worship through Eli, Samuel, and Solomon.

characters.name: Dust and Worms (teaching)
characters.purpose: Refutes, one by one, three named groups' specific reasons for denying the resurrection of the dead - the Sadducees (Seduqans, who say the soul does not survive death at all), the Samaritans (Samrans, who say the soul survives but the buried flesh cannot rise), and the Pharisees (Fereesans, who say God will unite souls with a different Heavenly flesh rather than the one that was buried) - insisting instead that the very flesh and soul that were separated at death will be reunited and judged together.

verses.note: States the Sadducee position: 'we will die tomorrow, mek us eat and drink, there is no joy we will see in the grave.'
States the Samaritan position: the soul is like wind and survives, but the flesh becomes dust and cannot rise.
States the Pharisee position: God will join souls to a different, Heavenly flesh rather than the buried body.
States the fuller Sadducee position: once the soul leaves the flesh, there is no resurrection of either.
Answers all three groups at length, insisting the very flesh that was buried will be raised and reunited with its own soul for judgement.

funFacts: Naming three distinct, explicitly-attributed afterlife positions this precisely is a real content difference from the standard KJV canon, where these groups' specific denial-of-resurrection views are described more briefly (e.g. Matthew 22:23, Acts 23:8).

characters.name: Master and Slave Alike (teaching)
characters.purpose: Describes the Day of Judgement itself - cosmic darkness, lightning, quaking, and hail - as the day every social rank (master and slave, king and pauper, parent and child, rich and poor) stands equal before God's sentence, each repaid strictly according to their own works rather than their earthly rank.

verses.note: Describes cosmic signs - total darkness, lightning, quaking, hail, and frost - accompanying the Day of Judgement.
States that on that day master and slave, king and pauper, parent and child stand equal before judgement.
Contrasts the reward awaiting the righteous (multiplied descendants, the Kingdom of Heaven) with the unending fire and 'worms that don't sleep' awaiting those who denied the resurrection.

characters.name: The Wheat Kernel (teaching)
characters.purpose: Offers everyday proofs that bodily resurrection is not absurd: fingernails and hair that keep regrowing after being cut, and a wheat kernel that must first be buried and 'destroyed' in the earth before it can rise as a full stalk of grain, extended further into a grapevine drawing up water, dew, and sun to bear fruit - both images likened to the soul being reunited with the body at the resurrection.

verses.note: Uses regrowing fingernails and hair as everyday evidence that the body can be restored after loss.
States that a wheat kernel cannot bear fruit unless it is first buried and 'destroyed' in the earth.
Extends the image to a grapevine drawing up water and sun to bear fruit, likened to the body-soul reunion at resurrection.

funFacts: The buried-and-destroyed wheat kernel image parallels the same figure used of Christ's death and resurrection in John 12:24, though this book applies it to all believers generally rather than to any single figure.

characters.name: Earth and Death's Harvest (teaching)
characters.purpose: Traces every human being's mortality back to Adam's own broken command, then turns to address Earth and Death directly as personified figures who have swallowed up every kind of person - noble and poor, beautiful and plain, warrior and singer alike - a repeated lament ('woe arisin from thee-I') on the total impartiality of the grave.

verses.note: Traces universal human death and burial back to Adam's breaking of God's command.
Addresses 'O Earth' directly, lamenting that it has swallowed nobles, kings, and beauties alike.
Addresses 'O death' directly in a repeated 'woe arisin from thee-I' refrain, noting death spares neither rich nor poor, kind nor evil.

characters.name: The Two Roads of the Soul (teaching)
characters.scribeTier: The Two Roads of the Soul
characters.purpose: Describes what happens the moment a soul leaves the body - Angels of Light escorting the righteous to the Garden, demons and Angels of Darkness dragging the wicked toward Gehenna - then warns rulers and the wealthy against hoarding money gained through fraud or interest, since it 'shall be rusted' and cannot be carried past death, closing the whole book with Moses' command to Joshua establishing cities of refuge as a final model of just, merciful rule, and a blessing on those who did God's will.

verses.note: Describes Angels of Light carrying righteous souls to the Garden, and demons/Angels of Darkness dragging the wicked toward Gehenna.
Warns that silver and gold gathered through fraud 'shall be rusted' and cannot benefit even the wicked's own children.
Recalls Moses commanding Joshua son of Nun to establish cities of refuge for those who kill by accident, as the LAW's own model of mercy.
Closes the book with a final blessing: those who did God's will 'shall be Irie with Him ina Him Kingdom foriva.'

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references to figures from other books, cited here only as historical exempla within the resurrection/kingship discourse - kept out of the character list above since they are not personally embodied within this book's own narrative.

historicalJudgesAndDeliverers.note: Cites Joshua (Iyasu), Gideon (Giedeon), Samson (Somson), Deborah (Deebora), Barak (Bariq), and Judith (Yodeet) as past deliverers God raised up for Israel during the sin-oppression-repentance cycle; each belongs to their own book's own character index.

balaamAndBalak.note: Cites Balak son of Zippor (Siefor child Balaq) hiring Balaam (Bele'am) to curse Israel, and Balaam's refusal, as a warning to kings; the full narrative belongs to Numbers' own character index.

mosesExempla.note: Cites Moses (Mussie) interceding for the sister and brother who criticized him (Numbers 12), Korah's rebellion (Qorie childran) being swallowed by the earth, and Moses and Aaron (Aron) building the Tabernacle furnishings, as models of humility versus rebellion; full narratives belong to Exodus/Leviticus/Numbers' own character indexes.

templeLineage.note: Cites Eli (Elyas), Samuel (Samu'iel), and Solomon (Selomon) as later stewards of God's Tabernacle/Temple worship in Jerusalem; not indexed individually here.

patriarchalOath.note: Repeated references to God's oath to the patriarchs Isaac (Yis'haq), Abraham (Abriham), and Jacob (Ya'iqob) as the basis for Israel's eventual forgiveness; not indexed individually here.

davidAndPsalm.note: Quotes David (Daweet) and the Psalms on the fleeting prosperity of the wicked and on wine gladdening the heart; not indexed individually here.

adamReference.note: Repeated references to Adam ('Adam) as the shared source of humanity's mortality and as the pattern for the resurrected wheat-kernel/body analogy; belongs to Genesis' own character index.
